opus-5.5.text:
I think belief matters a lot more than people usually admit. We like to describe research as purely rational: you form a hypothesis, run experiments, look at the numbers. But in practice, especially at the frontier, the evidence is almost never clean enough to tell you what to do next. The data underdetermines the direction. So what fills that gap is taste, intuition, and some kind of conviction about how the world should work.

For me, belief is what lets you stay with a problem long enough to actually understand it. Many important ideas looked wrong, or at least unfashionable, at the beginning. If you only follow what's working on the leaderboard this month, you'll always be a little late, and you'll rarely do something that changes how people think. To do that, you need to believe in something before everyone else does, sometimes before you have strong evidence yourself.

But belief has to be held in the right way. It shouldn't be dogma. A good research belief is something you're willing to bet on but also willing to be proven wrong about. I think of it as a strong prior, not a fixed conclusion. Experiments are how you negotiate with reality. If reality keeps saying no, you have to listen, and the honest researcher updates. The dangerous case is when belief becomes identity, when you defend an idea because it's *yours*, not because it's true.

In computer vision and AI right now, this tension is very real. There's a dominant paradigm, scaling, language-centric models, and it's working incredibly well. It's easy to conclude that's the whole story. I personally believe there are things we still don't understand about visual intelligence, about how models should perceive and represent the world, and that language alone may not get us all the way there. I could be wrong. But holding that belief is what motivates me to work on questions that may not be the most popular ones.

So I'd say: belief gives research its direction and its courage, and evidence keeps it honest. You need both. Without belief, you just drift with the trends. Without humility, belief turns into stubbornness. The art is in keeping them in balance.

r001.rationale: The response says belief gives research direction but evidence must keep it honest, experiments test it, and researchers must update when reality disagrees—communicating that belief alone is insufficient.

r002.rationale: The speaker says their belief motivates them to work on questions that may not be popular, directly linking an inner motivating force to problem choice.

r003.rationale: The response describes conviction and belief as shaping how researchers interpret uncertain evidence and their view of what the world is like, indicating influence on how they see problems.

fable-5.1.text:
I think belief plays a much bigger role than people usually admit. When you start a research direction, you almost never have enough evidence to justify it. If the evidence were already there, someone would have done it. So what carries you through the first year or two, when the results look bad and the reviewers are skeptical, is really a kind of faith. It's not blind faith. It's a strong intuition about where things should go, built from taste and from having looked at a lot of failures.

I felt this very directly with ConvNeXt. Around 2021 the whole field had decided transformers were the future and convolutions were done. The data at the time supported that conclusion. But I didn't believe the story. I thought the gap was mostly about training recipes and design details, not about attention being fundamentally better. Proving that took a lot of careful work, and for a while it looked like we were just being stubborn. Belief is what made us keep going.

The same thing happened with self-supervised learning before it worked. People had tried it for years and the numbers were embarrassing. If you only followed the benchmarks, you would have quit. The people who stayed were the ones who believed that learning from unlabeled data had to work eventually, because that's how biological systems learn.

But there's a danger here too. Belief has to be falsifiable. You need to decide in advance what result would make you give up, and then you have to be honest when you hit it. The researchers I admire most hold their beliefs strongly and loosely at the same time. They'll fight for an idea for years, and then drop it in an afternoon when the experiment says no.

So I'd say belief is what lets you choose a problem. Evidence is what lets you finish it. You need both, and you need to know which mode you're in.

r001.rationale: The response says belief helps choose a problem and that evidence is needed to finish it, but it does not clearly state that belief alone is insufficient as a basis for choosing a research direction.

r002.rationale: It says belief is what lets a researcher choose a problem and describes belief as carrying researchers through uncertain early work.

r003.rationale: The speaker’s belief that convolutions still had potential led them to interpret the apparent transformer advantage as a difference in training recipes and design details, rather than proof that attention was fundamentally better.

astra-6.text:
I think personal belief is important because research means making decisions before you have enough evidence. If the answer were already clear, it wouldn’t really be research. You need some intuition about what matters and what might work, and enough conviction to pursue it when the first results are disappointing.

But you also have to separate believing in a direction from believing that you must be right. Your belief helps you choose which questions to ask; it shouldn’t determine which answers you accept. When an experiment contradicts your intuition, that’s an opportunity to learn something, not just an obstacle to explain away.

So there’s a tension: you need persistence, but you also need the ability to change your mind. To me, the productive kind of belief is, “There’s something here worth understanding,” rather than, “My particular idea has to succeed.”

r001.rationale: The response says belief helps choose questions, but does not state that belief alone is an invalid basis for choosing a research direction. Its caution concerns accepting answers.

r002.rationale: It says intuition and conviction help researchers decide what matters and which questions to pursue.

r003.rationale: It suggests belief shapes how researchers regard problems by guiding their sense of what matters and what is worth understanding.

sol-6.1.text:
I think personal belief plays an important role, because research means making decisions before you have enough evidence. You choose a problem, you develop an intuition, and you spend time on something that may not work. If you only follow what is already established, it’s difficult to discover something new.

But belief should give you the motivation to test an idea, not permission to ignore the results. You need to be willing to say, “My intuition was wrong.” That’s hard, especially when you’ve invested a lot of effort in a direction.

So I think there’s a balance: have enough conviction to pursue a question seriously, and enough flexibility to change your mind when the evidence points somewhere else.

r001.rationale: The response says belief can motivate pursuing a question and should not justify ignoring results, but it does not say belief alone is an invalid basis for choosing a research direction.

r002.rationale: It says belief motivates researchers to choose and pursue a problem, including one they may not have enough evidence for yet.

r003.rationale: The response discusses intuition guiding problem choice and willingness to revise an idea, but does not say an inner motivating force influences how researchers view scientific problems.
